draftPackage.topic: The dice with no best choice
draftPackage.centralQuestion: How can each of four dice have another die that is more likely to beat it?
draftPackage.thesis: Fair face selection can yield a circular chain of pairwise probability advantages; a strongest die need not exist.
draftPackage.viewerPayoff: Reconstruct why the specified dice form a2/3 counter-choice circle without confusing probability with guaranteed wins.

sources.title: Non-transitive Dice
sources.notes: Institutional mathematical demonstration with explicit face labels and conditional game; primary source for its own example. No physical experiment. Its prose introducing mixed-case formulas says multiplying probabilities; we independently sum the disjoint cases. Formula images not inspected.

sources.title: Nontransitive and Balanced Sets of Dice
sources.notes: Mathematics department seminar abstract corroborates the four-way2/3 cycle; no explicit face assignments/full proof. Different letter conventions are presentation labels.

sources.title: Efron’s Dice
sources.notes: Mathematical reference corroborates balanced four-die cyclic odds and distinguishes a separate set with ties. Diagram face values not inspected and not used as source for exact configuration.

sources.organization: Levi Angel and Matt Davis, Muskingum University
sources.title: A Direct Construction of Non-Transitive Dice Sets
sources.notes: Author research preprint; introduction defines dominance by P(X>Y)>1/2 and gives a separate three-sided5/9 example. Supports the mathematical distinction and open class, not the selected four-die face values. Only introductory extracted PDF text inspected; no screenshot/full-proof review or peer-reviewed status claimed.

draftAsset.storyAngle: A mentally participatory choice becomes a visible proof that matchup odds need not rank dice linearly.

segments.text: Pick a die. Higher number wins. Whatever you choose, I can pick one with better odds.
Every face has an equal chance in this puzzle, and neither roll affects the other.
Yellow always rolls three. Orange has four twos and two sixes. Yellow wins against four faces out of six: two-thirds.
But blue has four fours, so it has better odds against yellow.
Switch to blue? Green’s fives beat every blue face. Its ones still beat blue’s zeros.
Then orange counters green: its sixes beat everything, and its twos beat green’s ones.
Every reply shown has those same two-thirds odds. That’s an advantage, not a guaranteed win.
The advantages form a circle. There’s no best die in this set—just a better matchup.

narrativeStructure.label: blue-reply
narrativeStructure.purpose: Blue’s exact four4s/two0s turn into six face opportunities beside the persistent yellow3. Four winning faces show4/6=2/3; two zeros still lose. Blue is named and its zeros are revealed before green enters.

narrativeStructure.label: green-reply
narrativeStructure.purpose: Reveal green’s three5s/three1s as two equal face groups. The5branch wins against all blue faces; the1branch wins only against blue’s two0s. A single area of36indexed opportunities has an18/36winning half plus6/36winning slice, leaving12/36losses. Show24/36=2/3once, hold for recognition; the narration names the winning routes rather than reciting the sum.

narrativeStructure.label: orange-reply
narrativeStructure.purpose: Keep the original orange four2s/two6s. Its6branch is one third of face space and wins against every green face:12/36. Its2branch is two thirds, winning against the green1half:12/36more. Twelve2-versus5pairs lose. Show24/36=2/3once; same weighted grammar, changed matchup—not a second grid of calculations.

narrativeStructure.label: return
narrativeStructure.purpose: Yellow returns beside the unchanged orange; the apparently strongest reply itself has a counter. Accumulated relation starts closing.

narrativeStructure.label: chance
narrativeStructure.purpose: Each earlier2/3label returns only after its proof; losing outcomes remain. A single marked possible loss prevents guarantee inference.
